A letter from the Governor

Dear Board Member,

On behalf of the members of the Board, it is my distinct privilege to welcome you to the Central Bank of Armenia.

Since its founding in the wake of Armenia’s independence, the Central Bank has played a fundamental role in supporting macroeconomic stability in Armenia. From overcoming the challenges of hyperinflation following the breakup of the Soviet Union to steering the economy through the successive crises of the 2020s, the Central Bank has remained steadfast in its commitment to providing the stability that the economy and society needs to grow and prosper. It is our firm belief that macroeconomic stability is among the most important preconditions for sustainable, long-term economic development and improving the wellbeing of Armenians over time.

Achieving this vision requires equal measures of discipline and innovation. Over the past three decades, we have made meaningful investments in our policymaking frameworks, aligning with, and at times setting, global best practice. Strong institutional frameworks, built upon robust analytics, Board-staff collaboration, and the very highest levels of transparency and accountability, are the foundation for how we maintain macroeconomic stability in Armenia. Perhaps the best illustration of this is the Central Bank’s development of the Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability—the world’s first framework for monetary policy as risk management, which we formally introduced in 2024.

As you embark on your journey as a member of the Board of the Central Bank of Armenia, I have no doubt that you appreciate the level of responsibility and public service that this new role carries. To support your seamless transition, we have prepared an onboarding package that will help you better understand Armenia’s modern economic history, the foundational principles of monetary policymaking, and the nuances of our policymaking framework.

Over the course of your term, I and the rest of the Board look forward to working closely with you to continue serving our mission to the Armenian people: to be a leading central bank, driven by research excellence and innovation. Your experience, expertise, and judgment will play an essential role in our continued ability to support price stability in Armenia.

Wishing you all the best,

Martin Galstyan
Governor, Central Bank of Armenia

Part I
The Great Inflation and the Transformation in Monetary Policy
Part I  ·  Chapter 1

Lessons from the 1970s: The Great Inflation

The story of modern monetary policy begins with a failure. This chapter examines how the post-war Keynesian consensus collapsed under the weight of the Great Inflation, what intellectual and policy mistakes made it possible, and how the painful correction that followed fundamentally reshaped the way central banks think and operate across the world.

Progress
Chapter 1
Chapter 2
Chapter 3
Why this chapter
matters

This chapter introduces the intellectual crisis that gave birth to modern central banking. Without understanding what went wrong in the 1970s and why, it is impossible to fully appreciate why the frameworks the CBA operates under today were designed the way they were. Virtually every principle of credibility, transparency, and forward-looking policy has its roots in the lessons of this era.

Before you beginThe events of the 1970s may feel distant, but their lessons are alive in every decision this institution makes. Watch this video not as history, but as the foundation on which everything the CBA does today was built.
01 The Great Inflation: Origins, Consequences, and Legacy 10 min
VP
Vazgen Poghosyan
Head of Monetary Policy Department, CBA

This video traces the intellectual and policy arc of the 1970s. It begins with the apparent stability of the Phillips Curve trade-off and the overconfidence it bred in policymakers, moves through the theoretical challenges posed by Friedman and Phelps, examines the compounding policy failures that allowed inflation to become entrenched, and concludes with Paul Volcker's decisive disinflation and the lasting institutional legacy it produced for central banks worldwide.

Phillips CurvePolicy credibilityVolcker disinflationInflation expectationsModern frameworks
Questions to Reflect On
  1. The Great Inflation was as much an intellectual failure as a policy failure. What does this tell us about the risks of over-relying on any single economic model or framework?
  2. Credibility, once lost by the Fed, took years of painful policy to recover. How does the CBA safeguard its own credibility today, and what would a loss of it cost Armenia?
  3. Volcker chose price stability over short-term political comfort. As a Board member, how do you think about the tension between institutional conviction and external pressure?

Part I  ·  Chapter 2

The Birth of Inflation Targeting: A New Era in Monetary Policy

By the late 1980s, the search for a durable nominal anchor had produced two complementary breakthroughs. New Zealand built the institutional architecture of inflation targeting. Canada built the analytical engine that made it work. This chapter traces those parallel innovations, from the Reserve Bank Act of 1989 to the world's first Forecasting and Policy Analysis System, and examines why credibility became the foundation of modern monetary policy.

Why this chapter
matters

The Great Inflation destroyed confidence in the frameworks that were supposed to maintain price stability. This chapter shows how two open economies rebuilt that confidence from the ground up: through institutional design and analytical innovation. Their work became the intellectual foundation on which every modern monetary policymaking framework now stands.

Before you beginVazgen Poghosyan explains not only the theoretical foundations behind the creation of the framework, but also the practical solutions that were responses to real failures, developed and adopted under real pressure.

History of Monetary Policy in Armenia

This chapter tells Armenia's monetary story from its most turbulent beginning. From the chaos of independence and hyperinflation, through a decade of monetary targeting, to the strategic transition that placed the CBA among a select group of small open economies that built both institutional and analytical credibility simultaneously.

Why this chapter
matters

This chapter is where Armenia's monetary history enters the journey. The CBA's story did not begin with a clean slate. It began in conditions of extraordinary difficulty: political uncertainty, economic collapse, and a public that had no reason yet to trust its institutions in a newly-independent country. Understanding where the CBA came from is inseparable from understanding what it has become.

Before you beginThese three videos tell a single continuous story: Armenia's own monetary journey from independence to a modern inflation targeting framework. Watch them in order. Each one builds directly on the last.
01 Armenia's Independence and the Hyperinflation Crisis 7 min

This video opens Armenia's monetary story at its most turbulent moment. Arthur Stepanyan, Manushak Grigoryan and Vahagn Grigoryan trace the economic reality that followed Armenia's declaration of independence on September 21, 1991, a country politically sovereign but economically dependent, still tied to the Soviet and Russian ruble. The shift to a market economy was anything but smooth: output collapsed, inflation spiraled, and public trust in the state eroded. They examine the factors that drove the CPI to 11,000% in 1993 alone, the delayed introduction of the Armenian dram on November 23 of that year, and the structural conditions that made stabilization so difficult. The video closes with the CBA's first independent monetary policy strategy in early 1994, the moment monetary policymaking in Armenia truly began.

What You Have Learned

You have now completed the first part of your learning journey. You began with the Great Inflation, a defining episode that exposed the limits of fine-tuning and the dangers of unanchored expectations. You then witnessed how two small open economies, New Zealand and Canada, rebuilt monetary credibility from the ground up through institutional and analytical innovation, giving birth to the inflation targeting frameworks that central banks operate under today. Finally, you followed Armenia's own monetary history from the earliest days of independence, through the chaos of hyperinflation, through a decade of monetary targeting, and to the strategic transition that established the CBA as a credible, forward-looking institution.

Principles of Inflation Targeting

Inflation targeting is not simply a numerical commitment. It rests on a set of interlocking principles that make policy credible, coherent, and effective. This chapter examines those principles through three focused videos, moving from the foundational role of the nominal anchor to the institutional design that allows central banks to translate analysis into action.

Part II  ·  Chapter 5

Monetary Policy Under Inflation Targeting in Armenia

Since adopting inflation targeting in 2006, the CBA has navigated an extraordinary succession of crises. Each episode tested the framework, shaped its evolution, and deepened the institution's understanding of what it means to conduct credible monetary policy in a small, open, and vulnerable economy. This chapter tells that story through four case studies.

Progress
Chapter 4
Chapter 5
Introductory Note

When the CBA adopted inflation targeting in 2006, both the global and the Armenian economies were in a highly expansionary period, with growth in the double-digits in Armenia through 2007. The adoption of full-fledged inflation targeting was not without challenges — the relative youth of the CBA as a credible institution, underdeveloped financial markets, and high dollarization all posed structural difficulties outside the direct scope of the CBA's influence. What was within scope was the institutional and operational setup for conducting policy analysis and communicating policy decisions. To that end, the CBA invested in FPAS, introducing its first macro model in 2007 and building the analytical infrastructure inflation targeting required.

Before you beginThe history in these videos is not distant. Some of the people who made these decisions are still in this institution. Some of the consequences are still being felt. Watch with that in mind.

This video examines the final episode in Part II, the period that made FPAS Mark II not just desirable but necessary. The sharp escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in February 2022 presented two genuinely divergent scenarios for Armenia. As the alternative scenario materialized, with large inflows of capital, people, and entrepreneurship driving 12.6% growth in 2022, the CBA executed a 650 basis point tightening cycle before beginning a conservative loosening in June 2023. This video examines the decisions made under profound uncertainty and the lessons they produced for the framework.

  2. The 2014 to 2015 Russian financial crisis destabilized inflation expectations almost overnight. How does the CBA's aggressive tightening and subsequent opportunistic disinflation inform your understanding of credibility as an institutional asset?

  5. Across all four episodes, the CBA maintained its 4% inflation objective on average. What does this achievement, earned through some of the most difficult conditions any small economy has faced, mean for your role as a Board member today?

Part III  ·  Chapter 6

The Intellectual Foundation of PRMAPS

This chapter introduces the conceptual core of the Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability. It begins with a clear-eyed diagnosis of why the world changed and why existing frameworks were no longer adequate. It then presents the least regrets model, the intellectual architecture that defines how the CBA thinks about monetary policy today.

Progress
Chapter 6
Chapter 7
Chapter 8
Chapter 9
Chapter 10
Chapter 11
Chapter 12
Why this chapter
matters

The Prudent Risk Management Approach did not emerge in a vacuum. It emerged from a fundamental question this CBA asked itself: is monetary policy about forecasting the most likely future, or is it about doing whatever is necessary to prevent the economy from sliding into dark corners?

Before you beginThis chapter is the intellectual core of Part III. The framework you are about to learn was not adopted from elsewhere. It was built here, at the Central Bank of Armenia, by the people around you.
01 Policy Imperatives in the Age of Uncertainty 9 min
VA
Vahe Avagyan
Advisor to the Governor, CBA

The world did not simply become more risky after 2020. It became structurally uncertain in ways that exposed a fundamental flaw in how central banks had been thinking about policy. But before examining that flaw, this video asks a more basic question: what is the fundamental role of monetary policy? The answer the CBA arrived at is unambiguous. Monetary policy is not primarily a forecasting exercise. Its fundamental purpose is to prevent the economy from sliding into dark corners, outcomes so adverse and so costly that they cannot be easily reversed. Vahe Avagyan examines the three layers of uncertainty that make this task so demanding: uncertainty about the state of the economy, uncertainty about its structure and the nonlinear relationships that linear models fail to capture, and the decision-making trap these uncertainties create. The temptation to resolve uncertainty by committing to a single baseline does not eliminate uncertainty. It amplifies it, ties the central bank's hands, and places its credibility at unnecessary risk.

UncertaintyData imperfectionNonlinearitiesEndogenous credibilityDark cornersLeast regretsScenario-based forward guidanceMarket reference scenarioTaxonomy of scenariosPRMAPS

Part III  ·  Chapter 7

The Role of Scenarios in Prudent Risk Management Framework

Under PRMAPS, scenarios are not a technical add-on to a central forecast. They are how the CBA structures its thinking, organizes its deliberations, and explains its decisions to the public and financial markets. This chapter traces the full architecture of scenario-based policymaking, from the principles that govern scenario selection to the market reference scenario that anchors it all.

Progress

Chapter 12
Why this chapter
matters

This chapter covers how scenarios are defined, selected, structured, and anchored under PRMAPS, from the Three R's to the Market Reference Scenario.

Before you beginThis chapter shows how the CBA defines, selects, and constructs scenarios under PRMAPS.
01 Defining Scenarios Under PRMAPS vs Traditional Frameworks 5 min
HA
Hayk Avetisyan
Director of the Macroeconomic Directorate, CBA

In traditional monetary policy frameworks, scenarios are used to test the sensitivity of a baseline forecast to alternative assumptions. Under PRMAPS, their purpose is fundamentally different. Hayk Avetisyan explains how the Taxonomy of Scenarios defines scenarios as plausible economic and financial developments not currently priced in financial markets, whose purpose is to identify the policy-relevant risks that, if left unmanaged, could result in policy errors and push the economy toward dark corners. These are not deviations from a central view. They are realistic outcomes that cause genuine concern for policymakers, structured within a classification that distinguishes between developments requiring tighter policy and those requiring looser policy, both relative to the market reference scenario. Critically, under PRMAPS, it is the Board that develops the full set of scenarios in the Taxonomy of Scenarios, not staff. Two illustrative scenarios are then selected at near-random for quantification and communication purposes, ensuring that the CBA's published scenarios do not reveal policymakers' preferences about the most likely outcome.

Taxonomy of scenariosMarket reference scenarioNear-random selectionPRMAPS vs traditional frameworks
02 Defining the Appropriate Set of Scenarios: The Three R's 4 min
HA
Hayk Avetisyan
Director of the Macroeconomic Directorate, CBA

When thinking about potential scenarios regarding how the economy might develop, there is a virtually limitless universe of scenarios that one could imagine, especially in times of higher uncertainty. But having an exceedingly broad list that represents every possible development does not add value; it merely bombards decision-makers and external audiences with unnecessary information, and it certainly does not aid policymakers in managing uncertainty. Therefore, scenarios that are put on the table for discussion of policy risks must be selected according to a well-defined set of rules and systematized according to a consistent structure, which can help policymakers best understand the realistic, data-driven, and policy-relevant issues that they must manage to ensure medium-term price stability.

Three R'sRelatedRelevantRealisticPolicy-relevant risk
03 Taxonomy of Scenarios and Selection of Illustrative Scenarios 10 min
VP
Vazgen Poghosyan
Head of Monetary Policy Department, CBA

The scenarios, which are all rooted in data, realistic, and relevant for policy, are organized within a structured and consistent framework. A formal classification system, termed the Taxonomy of Scenarios, is especially helpful for motivating the development of 3R-consistent scenarios as well as allowing policymakers and external audiences to understand the implications these scenarios would have on monetary policy. To support both classification and communication, each scenario is summarized as a concise narrative statement that describes the event and its underlying cause, followed by a brief discussion of the macroeconomic consequences and policy implications. In each policymaking round, one Case A and one Case B scenario is selected to be quantified as a full-fledged economic scenario with macro-consistent projections across a wide array of variables. These quantified scenarios are illustrative in nature, meaning that they do not represent what the staff or Board believes to be the most likely or the most preferable future scenario.

Taxonomy of ScenariosClassification systemNarrative structureCase ACase B3R-consistent scenariosIllustrative scenariosCase A and Case BNear-random selectionMacro-consistent projectionsExternal communications
04 The Market Reference Scenario 7 min
VP
Vazgen Poghosyan
Head of Monetary Policy Department, CBA

Treating monetary policy as a risk management process requires a different approach to the scenario-building process. Rather than treating its own central projections as the best piece of information and forcing market participants to coalesce around this singular view of unfolding economic conditions, the CBA instead utilizes market expectations for the central bank policy rate as a starting point for policy deliberations. Market expectations, by design, contain significant information about market views on current economic developments and possible behavior of monetary policy in the future economic environment. Under the PRMAPS framework, the CBA relies on the Market Reference Scenario, a macro-consistent scenario that captures market expectations of the future economic outlook, around which Case A and Case B scenarios are constructed.

Market Reference ScenarioMarket expectationsPolicy rate pathMacro-consistent projectionsCase A and Case B scenarios
Questions to Reflect On
  1. The Three R's are designed to discipline scenario selection. As a Board member, how do you apply this discipline when faced with a scenario that feels important but may not meet all three criteria?
  2. Illustrative scenarios are selected at near-random and do not represent the Board's preferred view of the future. How does this design choice strengthen the CBA's credibility and communication with financial markets?
  3. The Market Reference Scenario uses market expectations rather than the CBA's own projections as its starting point. What are the advantages and limits of this approach in a small open economy like Armenia?

Part III  ·  Chapter 8

Institutional Arrangements and Processes of the PRMAPS Framework

The core ideas of the prudent risk management approach, including least regrets decision-making, monetary policy as risk management, scenario-based analysis, and high degrees of transparency and accountability, are general principles, and these can be applied within an institutional framework in a number of ways. The CBA has institutionalized the prudent risk management approach within a holistic and comprehensive operational framework known as FPAS Mark II (representing the second generation of the Forecasting and Policy Analysis System). FPAS Mark II represents how the prudent risk management approach is put into practice on an operational, institutional, and procedural level, and this chapter is devoted to exploring the nuts and bolts, day-to-day aspects of putting the prudent risk management approach into practice at the CBA.

02 Weekly Analytical Briefings 2 min
AP
Anzhela Papikyan
Macroeconomic Policy Expert, CBA

At the heart of the processes supporting the policy decisions are weekly analytical briefings to the Board by the Staff. These weekly briefings take place, without fail, every Wednesday afternoon, ensuring that the monetary policymaking process and the discussion of the key risks and uncertainties is a continuous process that is not confined to the days or weeks leading up to each decision. The weekly briefings are intended to provide a platform for the Staff to present to, and discuss with, the Board the most important policy-relevant issues and analysis that inform high-quality decisions. Each week, the staff selects a topic that it deems to be particularly relevant from a policy perspective (e.g. labor market conditions in Armenia, global commodity price developments, the service sector in Armenia, and so on), prepares high-quality analysis, and presents it to the Board.

Weekly briefingsWednesday briefingsContinuous policymakingPolicy-relevant analysisBoard-Staff interactionAnalytical disciplineFPAS Mark II
03 Board-Staff Collaboration 6 min
VP
Vazgen Poghosyan
Head of Monetary Policy Department, CBA

The successful functioning of the framework in practice depends not just on processes and procedures; it most of all relies on effective human capital — among both decision-makers and economists — to ensure that its practical, real-life application works in service of its objectives. In many ways, this is about the culture of the CBA's Board and its Monetary Policy Department. While culture is often intangible and immeasurable, the combination of strong leadership and vision from the institution's highest levels with systematic, institutional arrangements governing internal relationships, processes, and communications can go a long way in helping cultivate this desired corporate culture. For the Board, the ability to devise policies of least regrets — which derive from robust deliberations around a diverse array of perspectives — depends upon fostering a culture of adversarial collaboration (Kahneman) that is explicitly designed to avoid groupthink and consensus seeking. For the Staff, whose key role is supporting the Board, through high-quality analysis, to make informed policy decisions, the emphasis is on professionalism, analytical rigor, and critical thinking (“parallel/lateral thinking” per de Bono). This section explores this culture in practice, as well as practical arrangements governing the delineation of responsibilities between the Board and the staff.

Adversarial collaborationBoard cultureStaff professionalismLateral thinkingRole delineationGroupthink prevention

“I'd rather have Bob Solow than an econometric model, but I'd rather have Bob Solow with an econometric model than without one.”— Paul Samuelson

The tools in this chapter exist for this exact reason. They do not replace judgment. They sharpen it.

Before you beginSamuelson's point was not that models are unimportant. It was that judgment always comes first. With that in mind, what matters here is understanding what each tool is designed to do, why it was built the way it was, and how it supports the quality of analysis that reaches the Board.
01 Measurement Proxies for Price Stability: Non-Traded Sticky Price Inflation 6 min
AP
Anzhela Papikyan
Macroeconomic Policy Expert, CBA

Although the headline CPI remains the key inflation indicator to follow from the monetary policy perspective, different components of it matter for a detailed and thorough discussion and communication of policy decisions, especially in the framework of risk management. The key question comes in how should we decompose the CPI to better help monetary policymakers make better decisions and communicate policy more effectively? This question was put at the core of the research for Non-Traded Sticky Price Inflation, where a decomposition of the CPI is designed from the perspective of the modern monetary policy transmission mechanism with an emphasis on supply factor and exchange-rate driven flexible components and more demand and inflation-expectations driven sticky components.

NTSPISticky pricesFlexible pricesDemand-driven inflationPolicy communication
02 Macroeconomic Modeling Toolkit 7 min
AA
Ani Asoyan
Macroeconomic Policy Expert, CBA

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the global policy landscape has been shaped by a persistent and elevated level of uncertainty. This uncertainty has been exacerbated by multiple overlapping shocks, including geopolitical tensions, energy price volatility, supply chain disruptions, and more. These developments have fundamentally challenged the usefulness of baseline projections, as the world economy has become increasingly susceptible to non-linear, high-impact tail events. The macroeconomic modeling toolkit used to support the framework at the CBA therefore includes the following three layers: ENDOCRED, the analytical tool with crucial nonlinearities and endogenous credibility, used to quantify the illustrative scenarios; QPM, a linear model used for filtering history and discussing unobservables in a consistent manner; and GPM, a three-country model covering the US, EU, and Russia plus commodities including oil, copper, and food, used for analyzing the external sector.

ENDOCREDQPMGPMNonlinearitiesModeling under uncertainty

Non-Tradeable Sticky Price Inflation: Developing Better Concepts for Monetary Policy Analysis

Angela Papikyan, Hayk Avetisyan, and Douglas Laxton — Central Bank of Armenia, December 2023 · CBA Working Paper 2023/19

This paper develops the conceptual basis for Non-Traded Sticky Price Inflation and provides the methodology for constructing NTSPI for Armenia, exploring how it can be incorporated within modern monetary policy frameworks that include a loss function and endogenous credibility.

Access the paper →
Recommended Reading

An analytical framework to support a prudent risk management approach in Armenia

Ani Asoyan, Jared Laxton — CBA Working Paper WP-2026-03

The paper develops and documents the Central Bank of Armenia’s evolving analytical framework for monetary policy analysis under uncertainty and the prudent risk-management approach. It introduces the EndoCred framework, which extends the CBA’s Quarterly Projection Model (QPM) to better support scenario-based risk analysis by incorporating endogenous monetary policy credibility, nonlinear inflation dynamics, and richer transmission mechanisms, including financial dollarization, long-term interest rates, and term premia. In this context, EndoCred is not intended as a mechanical policy rule, but rather as a complementary analytical tool for scenario design, risk assessment, and structuring monetary policy judgment.

Part III  ·  Chapter 10

Human Capital Framework

With the development of new approaches to monetary policy decision-making in PRMAPS, a unique opportunity emerges to rethink not only how monetary policymaking is conducted and communicated, but also what role human capital ought to play in this revitalized system. The development of human capital is a fundamental priority of the CBA. Under the risk management approach, the main role of the staff is to prepare professional economic analysis that provides a comprehensive view of the macro environment and possible parallel scenarios. Under this approach, critical thinking and synthesizing economic developments, processes, and behaviors are among the most important professional characteristics of a team member. Achieving this type of team and professional culture requires having in place a systematic vision and framework for developing human capital in the monetary policy department.

The quality of analysis that supports well-informed decision making is ultimately determined by the quality of the people who produce it. The CBA's Monetary Policy Department has fundamentally restructured its human capital framework under FPAS Mark II, moving away from unnecessary hierarchy and narrow specialization toward a culture built around the universal economist: a critical thinker capable of contributing meaningfully at every stage of the policymaking process.

02 Team Structure and Dynamic Learning Environment 8 min
VP
Vazgen Poghosyan
Head of Monetary Policy Department, CBA

MPD staff are divided each year into four teams of six economists, which rotate roles every quarter. Over the course of the year, each team is responsible for one full policymaking cycle, which includes one interim decision and one quarterly decision. During the remaining three quarters of the year, team members carry out work arising from their individual development plans, such as economic research, training, and projects aimed at improving the quality of the framework. To enable this rotation of roles and promote staff development, the generalist economist principle has been established, which values the acquisition of broad knowledge over narrow specialization. We aim to build an institutional culture in the Monetary Policy Department that encourages the continuous learning and development of staff. This Dynamic Learning Environment is characterized by its intensity, as well as by high professional and collaborative standards. Its goal is to have macroeconomists who meet the highest professional standards and requirements in the world. Key pillars of this approach include fostering critical thinking, continuous learning, knowledge sharing, and providing feedback.

Team structureRotational systemGeneralist economistsDynamic Learning EnvironmentCollaborative cultureCritical thinkingPeer learningConstructive feedback

Communications and Transparency Framework

Effective monetary policy communication serves to clarify the policy stance, its rationale, and future directions for both financial markets and the general public, with the core objective of eliminating uncertainty about the central bank's commitment to price stability and keeping inflation expectations well-anchored. The CBA's communications framework is designed to make the policymaking process understandable, reliable, and accountable, building on global best practices while introducing new approaches that reflect the heightened emphasis on openly communicating risks and uncertainties inherent in the policymaking process.

Under the prudent risk management approach to policymaking, accountability cannot be about determining whether forecasts were well-constructed or why they deviated from actual outcomes. Instead, accountability is about understanding and explaining how the central bank thought about the key sources of risk and uncertainty that threatened price stability, and how they responded to and sought to manage these scenarios in order to achieve their constitutional mandate.
