Appendix

Further Reading and Viewing

Optional — for those who want to go deeper.

I. Intellectual foundations and the historical overview
1
Paul A. Samuelson and Robert M. Solow, "Analytical Aspects of Anti-Inflation Policy" (1960)
SOURCE · JSTOR stable article page →

Samuelson and Solow present the influential interpretation of the relationship between unemployment and inflation that preceded the Great Inflation. The original contribution contains qualifications that are often absent from later summaries. It nevertheless clarifies the basis on which policymakers came to view aggregate demand management as providing a durable choice between inflation and employment outcomes.

Recommended focus: The discussion of the observed relationship between inflation and unemployment, together with the concluding policy implications.

2
Milton Friedman, "The Role of Monetary Policy" (1968)
SOURCE · American Economic Association · full article →

Friedman explains why monetary policy cannot maintain unemployment permanently below its sustainable level and why an apparently stable relationship between inflation and unemployment changes as expectations adjust. The article provides a foundation for the modern understanding of inflation expectations, the natural rate and the limitations of discretionary fine tuning.

Recommended focus: The sections on what monetary policy can and cannot accomplish and the discussion of the natural rate.

3
Michael D. Bordo and Athanasios Orphanides, "Introduction," in The Great Inflation: The Rebirth of Modern Central Banking (2013)
SOURCE · NBER · official chapter in full →  ·  SOURCE · volume and contents →

The introduction provides a comprehensive synthesis of the literature. It distinguishes among monetary accommodation, supply shocks, deficient policy doctrine, mismeasurement of economic capacity, institutional pressures and international monetary conditions. The cross country evidence further shows why similar external shocks produced different inflation outcomes.

Recommended focus: The full introduction, pages 1 to 22.

4
John B. Taylor, "The Great Inflation, the Great Disinflation, and Policies for Future Price Stability" (1992)
SOURCE · Reserve Bank of Australia · full conference paper →

Taylor reviews the rise and reversal of inflation across the United States, Germany, Japan and other economies. The paper examines why governments tolerated inflation despite recognizing its costs and relates the historical record to the design of more predictable policy. Taylor was also among the senior economists who advised the development of the CBA's prudent risk management framework.

Recommended focus: Sections 1 and 2 and the concluding historical lessons; the econometric sections may be omitted.

5
Athanasios Orphanides, "The Road to Price Stability" (2006)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · publication page and full paper →

Orphanides reconstructs the transition from Volcker's declaration of war on inflation to the consolidation of price stability under Greenspan. Drawing extensively on the historical record, the paper examines the evolution of policy judgment, communication and commitment rather than relying on a formal model. It complements the overview by Bordo and Orphanides and reflects the work of an economist whose advice is acknowledged in the CBA volume.

Recommended focus: The historical narrative and the concluding discussion of the conditions required to preserve price stability.

6
Guy Debelle and Douglas Laxton, "Is the Phillips Curve Really a Curve? Some Evidence for Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States" (1996)
SOURCE · IMF Working Paper →

Debelle and Laxton test whether the Phillips curve is convex, finding that a given fall in unemployment below the NAIRU raises inflation by more than an equivalent rise in unemployment lowers it. The result implies that a central bank which fails to stabilise the business cycle will induce a permanently higher natural rate of unemployment, reinforcing the case against the discretionary fine tuning that contributed to the Great Inflation. Laxton was later among the senior economists who advised the development of the CBA's prudent risk management framework.

Recommended focus: The statement of the convexity result and its policy implications in the introduction and conclusion; the econometric and NAIRU-filtering sections may be omitted.

7
Charles Freedman and Douglas Laxton, "Why Inflation Targeting?" (2009)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · publication page and full paper →

Freedman and Laxton connect the breakdown of the long term Phillips curve relationship to the adoption of a nominal anchor and a full inflation targeting framework. The proposed assignment concerns the institutional argument and practical explanation rather than the formal material. It establishes the intellectual lineage of the framework that preceded FPAS Mark II.

Recommended focus: The sections on the costs of inflation, the need for a nominal anchor and the defining elements of inflation targeting.

II. Firsthand accounts from monetary policymakers
8
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Helmut Schlesinger, "Recent Experiences with Monetary Policy in the Federal Republic of Germany" (1976)
SOURCE · Duncker & Humblot · bilingual article and complete PDF →

Writing as a member of the Bundesbank Directorate during the Great Inflation, Schlesinger explains how the move to floating exchange rates widened the scope for an independent policy directed toward price stability. The German case provides a counterpoint to the United States. Comparable external shocks produced different outcomes under different monetary institutions, policy priorities and responses to inflation.

Recommended focus: The English language account of the policy regime after 1973 and the concluding institutional lessons.

9
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Arthur F. Burns, "The Anguish of Central Banking" (1979)
SOURCE · Per Jacobsson Foundation · full lecture →

Burns chaired the Federal Reserve during much of the Great Inflation. His lecture describes the political pressures, fiscal conditions, social demands and prevailing ideas that he considered constraints on central bank action. The account shows how recognition of the inflation problem may coexist with an inadequate policy response.

Recommended focus: Burns's diagnosis of institutional constraints and his account of the limits of central bank independence.

10
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Paul A. Volcker, Statement before the Joint Economic Committee (17 October 1979)
SOURCE · FRASER, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis · official statement in full →

Delivered shortly after the Federal Reserve announced its October 1979 changes to operating procedures, this statement provides a contemporaneous explanation of the regime shift. Volcker addresses inflation expectations, policy credibility, the external value of the dollar, the need for persistence and the complementary role of fiscal discipline before the outcome of the disinflation was known.

Recommended focus: The opening diagnosis, the explanation of the October measures and the concluding discussion of policy persistence.

11
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Paul A. Volcker and Christine Harper, Keeping At It: The Quest for Sound Money and Good Government (2018)
SOURCE · PublicAffairs · official publisher page →

Volcker's memoir is the principal personal retrospective on the disinflation. It describes the political and institutional environment, the importance assigned to price stability and the pressures surrounding the major decisions. The account illustrates the exercise of judgment and public responsibility, including the acceptance of criticism in the near term in pursuit of lasting stability.

Recommended focus: The chapters covering Volcker's appointment as Federal Reserve Chair, the October 1979 policy change and the subsequent disinflation.

12
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Ben S. Bernanke, "A Century of U.S. Central Banking: Goals, Frameworks, Accountability" (2013)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech →  ·  SOURCE · AEA · complimentary full text →

Bernanke provides an authoritative retrospective by a serving Federal Reserve Chair. His discussion relates excessive optimism about productive capacity, interpretations centred on cost pressures, insufficient monetary restraint and weakly anchored expectations to the subsequent development of policy frameworks, transparency and accountability.

Recommended focus: The Great Inflation and Volcker disinflation sections and the concluding discussion of accountability and communication.

13
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA FRAMEWORK CONTRIBUTOR
David J. Archer, "Inflation Targeting in New Zealand" (2000)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · full presentation →

Archer, then Assistant Governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, explains how inflation targeting emerged from institutional reform and practical experience rather than from a fully specified academic design. He addresses the statutory objective, the relationship between government and the central bank, transparency, accountability and policy formulation based on prospective conditions. The CBA volume identifies Archer's later discussions with Martin Galstyan and Douglas Laxton as an early contribution to the current framework.

Recommended focus: Sections I and II and the concluding assessment of institutional design, flexibility and accountability.

14
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Don Brash, "Practical Experiences in Reducing Inflation: The Case of New Zealand" (2013)
SOURCE · NBER · full chapter →

Brash draws on nearly fourteen years as Governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. He describes the transition from high inflation and extensive controls to exchange rate flexibility, operational independence and the first formal inflation targeting regime. The case demonstrates that credibility depends on a coherent institutional and fiscal framework, rather than on a numerical target alone.

Recommended focus: The account of the reforms from 1984 to 1990, the adoption of inflation targeting and the practical sources of credibility.

15
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
John Crow, "Practical Experiences in Reducing Inflation: The Case of Canada" (2013)
SOURCE · NBER · full chapter →

Crow provides a firsthand account of the Bank of Canada's strategy for reducing inflation and its institutional transition toward inflation targeting. The chapter examines the relationship among the governor, the finance ministry, statutory authority and public communication during a contested disinflation.

Recommended focus: The sections on the Bank's authority to act, relations with the government and the public articulation of price stability.

16
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Jacob A. Frenkel, "Interview with Jacob Frenkel" (1993)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis · full interview →

Speaking while Governor of the Bank of Israel, Frenkel discusses the institutional and policy requirements for sustaining Israel's stabilisation after a period of high inflation. The interview integrates central bank independence, fiscal discipline, the nominal anchor and the exchange rate framework in the account of a policymaker responsible for disinflation in a small open economy.

Recommended focus: The discussion of inflation, fiscal policy, the exchange rate band and the relationship between the Bank of Israel and the government.

17
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA APPLICATION
Martin Galstyan, "Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: The Role of Policy Credibility" (2022)
SOURCE · IMF Annual Meetings · Governor Talk, report and recording →  ·  SOURCE · CBA · presentation →

Governor Galstyan sets out the institutional lesson that the CBA draws from episodes in which monetary policy has fallen behind the curve. Forecast error and nonlinear outcomes are treated as central features of the policy problem rather than as marginal complications. The discussion explains the CBA's transition from a single baseline framework toward scenarios, prudent risk management and decisions guided by the principle of least regrets.

Recommended focus: The full Governor Talk and the presentation sections on credibility, dark corners and multiple scenarios.

III. Historical interpretation and comparative cases
18
J. Bradford DeLong, "America's Peacetime Inflation: The 1970s" (1997)
SOURCE · NBER · full chapter →

DeLong's accessible historical account emphasises how the memory of the Great Depression led policymakers to place greater weight on avoiding unemployment than on containing an initially gradual increase in inflation. The chapter combines political history, economic ideas and institutional incentives and illustrates how the lessons of one crisis may distort the response to the next.

Recommended focus: The historical narrative and the concluding interpretation; detailed quantitative material may be omitted.

19
Christina D. Romer and David H. Romer, "The Evolution of Economic Understanding and Postwar Stabilization Policy" (2002)
SOURCE · NBER publication page →  ·  SOURCE · full text provided by the author →

Romer and Romer examine how policymakers' changing beliefs about potential output, inflation and aggregate demand affected actual policy. Their broader institutional lesson is important for a Board audience: serious policy errors may arise from a confidently held but incorrect interpretation of the economy rather than from a lack of commitment or analytical effort.

Recommended focus: The sections on the 1960s and 1970s and the comparison with the subsequent change in policy doctrine.

20
Thomas J. Sargent, "The Ends of Four Big Inflations" (1982)
SOURCE · NBER · chapter page and complete download →

Sargent studies the Austrian, German, Hungarian and Polish stabilisations after the First World War. Although these inflations were more extreme than the Great Inflation, the comparative cases establish that durable stabilisation may require a credible change in the broader monetary and fiscal regime, rather than an isolated interest rate decision.

Recommended focus: The comparative historical narratives and concluding synthesis; formal discussion may be omitted.

IV. Contemporary institutional relevance
21
Kenneth S. Rogoff, "Globalization and Global Disinflation" (2003)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · full Jackson Hole paper →

Rogoff asks whether the global fall in inflation reflected better central banking alone or also a more favourable environment created by globalisation, deregulation and competition. The paper adds an important qualification to institutional success stories: policymakers should distinguish achievements generated by the regime from favourable structural forces that may later reverse.

Recommended focus: The introduction, the global disinflation narrative and the concluding discussion of risks to the environment of low inflation. The stylised model may be omitted.

22
Kenneth S. Rogoff, "The Age of Inflation: Easy Money, Hard Choices" (2022)
SOURCE · Foreign Affairs · article page →

Rogoff uses the inflation surge following the pandemic to reconsider the lessons of the 1970s. The article explains how sustained political and fiscal pressure may weaken central bank independence before any formal change in the mandate. The analysis bears directly on the institutional resilience required to preserve price stability.

Recommended focus: The full article.

23
Lawrence H. Summers, "The Inflation Risk Is Real" (2021)
SOURCE · Author's website · full article →

Summers was among the earliest prominent policymakers and economists to argue that the policy mix following the pandemic created a material risk of persistent inflation, rather than a transitory change in relative prices. The article records a contemporaneous dissenting diagnosis made before the inflation outcome was known. The CBA volume uses this debate to illustrate the importance of evaluating competing interpretations and asymmetric policy risks.

Recommended focus: The full article, read as a contemporaneous policy argument rather than a retrospective assessment.

24
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA FRAMEWORK INFLUENCE
Alan Greenspan, "Risk and Uncertainty in Monetary Policy" (2004)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech →

Greenspan presents monetary policy as decision making under pervasive uncertainty, with explicit attention to the probability and cost of alternative errors. The CBA volume identifies the speech as an early influence on the prudent risk management approach. It also records how the Federal Reserve interpreted the lessons of the Great Inflation and the limitations of fine tuning.

Recommended focus: The discussion of policy as risk management, uncertainty about economic structure and the historical examples of asymmetric risks.

25
William R. White, "Is Price Stability Enough?" (2006)
SOURCE · Bank for International Settlements · publication page and full paper →

White recognizes the substantial benefits of disinflation while cautioning that stability in consumer prices does not by itself ensure macroeconomic or financial stability. The paper broadens the institutional lesson without weakening the priority assigned to price stability. White is among the senior international experts whose feedback is acknowledged in the CBA volume.

Recommended focus: The historical discussion and the concluding implications for flexible policy over a longer horizon.

26
Federal Reserve History, "Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls" (essay)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve History · full essay →

The essay explains how the August 1971 decision to suspend dollar convertibility to gold, alongside the first peacetime wage-price freeze in U.S. history, ended the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates. It records the domestic inflation pressure and the international gold run that jointly motivated the decision, and traces the subsequent path from the Smithsonian Agreement to generalized floating by 1973.

Recommended focus: The full essay; it is a concise institutional narrative written for general reference and requires no supplementary reading.

27
Michael D. Bordo and Barry Eichengreen, "Bretton Woods and the Great Inflation" (2008)
SOURCE · NBER · full working paper →

Bordo and Eichengreen argue that the acceleration of US inflation after 1965 reflected a shift in responsibility for the balance of payments away from the Federal Reserve and toward the Treasury, which freed the Fed to pursue domestic objectives more aggressively once external monetary discipline no longer constrained it. The paper connects the international monetary story to the domestic policy failures covered elsewhere in this chapter.

Recommended focus: The introduction and the concluding assessment of how the erosion of the gold-standard constraint changed Federal Reserve incentives; the FOMC minutes analysis may be treated as supporting evidence.

28
Alan S. Blinder and Jeremy B. Rudd, "The Supply-Shock Explanation of the Great Stagflation Revisited" (2008)
SOURCE · NBER · full working paper →

Blinder and Rudd reassess the classic supply-shock account of the 1973--74 and 1978--80 inflation spikes, attributing both largely to food and energy price shocks and, in 1973--74, the removal of Nixon-era price controls. The paper directly engages critics who assign primary responsibility to monetary policy instead, giving the Board a rigorous treatment of how much of the Great Inflation is properly attributed to supply shocks versus policy choices.

Recommended focus: The statement of the classic supply-shock explanation and the rebuttal of the monetary-policy-only view; the later discussion of why recent oil shocks have smaller effects may be omitted.

29
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Piti Disyatat, "Targeting Inflation (More) Flexibly" (2024)
SOURCE · Bank for International Settlements · full speech →

Disyatat, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Thailand, explains how credibility acquired through successful disinflation can permit flexibility when inflation is driven by sector specific or global changes in relative prices. The speech provides a contemporary counterpart to the experience of the 1970s. Flexibility is sustainable only when the regime of low inflation and the central bank's response to genuine persistence remain credible.

Recommended focus: The full speech, comprising four pages.

30
David Archer, Martin Galstyan and Douglas Laxton, "FPAS Mark II: Avoiding Dark Corners and Eliminating the Folly in Baselines and Local Approximations" (2022)
SOURCE · CBA · publication page →  ·  SOURCE · CBA · full working paper →

The paper sets out the initial public case for the CBA's move from a single baseline forecasting framework toward multiple scenarios, nonlinear analysis and monetary policy as risk management. In the context of Chapter 1, it demonstrates how the risk of delayed or excessively confident policy responses has been reflected in the design of the CBA's current decision framework.

Recommended focus: The abstract, introduction and conceptual sections on dark corners, baselines and monetary policy as risk management; the technical appendices may be omitted.

31
Douglas Laxton, Hayk Avetisyan and Vahe Avagyan, eds., Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: Theory and Practice at the Central Bank of Armenia (2026)
SOURCE · CBA · publication page →  ·  SOURCE · CBA · full book →

The CBA volume connects the experience of the Great Inflation with the current Armenian framework. Its discussion of Volcker, policy credibility, uncertainty and the avoidance of severely adverse outcomes shows how the historical lessons inform the CBA's prudent risk management approach.

Recommended focus: The Foreword and the sections discussing the Great Inflation, inflation expectations and monetary policy as risk management.

V. Deeper reference
32
Allan H. Meltzer, A History of the Federal Reserve, Volume 2, Book 2: 1970--1986 (2010)
SOURCE · University of Chicago Press · official book page →

Meltzer provides the principal archival history of Federal Reserve policymaking from the Burns era through Volcker. The volume reconstructs internal debates, operating procedures, political relationships and changes in doctrine. It is the main reference for detailed study rather than an assigned Board reading.

Source links were verified on 10 August 2026. Availability may subsequently change on publisher or institutional websites.

I. Institutional foundations and the design of inflation targeting
1
Frederic S. Mishkin, "International Experiences with Different Monetary Policy Regimes" (1999)
SOURCE · NBER working paper and full text →

Mishkin provides a comparative account of exchange rate pegs, monetary targeting and inflation targeting. The analysis establishes that an effective nominal anchor requires supporting institutional arrangements, public accountability and a strategy consistent with the country's economic structure and policy history.

Recommended focus: Introduction, the discussion of inflation targeting, and the concluding lessons on institutional prerequisites.

2
IMF EDITED VOLUME
Tobias Adrian, Douglas Laxton and Maurice Obstfeld, eds., "Advancing the Frontiers of Monetary Policy" (International Monetary Fund, 2018)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · full book →

Fourteen chapters by IMF economists synthesise a quarter-century of inflation-forecast targeting, combining first-principles chapters with country case studies including the Czech Republic, India and the United States. Several sources elsewhere in this reading list, including Governor Galstyan's own account of the CBA's framework, draw directly on the thinking developed in this volume.

Recommended focus: Chapter 1 (overview), Chapter 2 (first principles) and Chapter 14 (a robust and adaptable nominal anchor); individual country chapters may be read selectively according to Board member interest.

3
Maurice Obstfeld and Kenneth Rogoff, "The Mirage of Fixed Exchange Rates" (1995)
SOURCE · NBER working paper and full text →

Obstfeld and Rogoff explain why adjustable pegs are vulnerable when capital is mobile and policy credibility is incomplete. For a small open economy, the essay establishes the strategic case for combining exchange rate flexibility with a credible domestic nominal anchor rather than treating the exchange rate as an independent and continuously defensible objective.

Recommended focus: The conceptual argument on the fragility of soft pegs and the policy implications for open economies.

4
Guillermo A. Calvo and Frederic S. Mishkin, "The Mirage of Exchange Rate Regimes for Emerging Market Countries" (2003)
SOURCE · NBER working paper and full text →

Calvo and Mishkin shift the discussion from regime labels to the institutional conditions that determine whether a framework can endure. They emphasise fiscal discipline, financial sector soundness, institutional credibility and the capacity to withstand external shocks. The paper is therefore directly relevant to Board oversight of a monetary policy framework in an emerging market.

Recommended focus: The institutional diagnosis and the concluding recommendations for emerging market economies.

5
Andrea Schaechter, Mark R. Stone and Mark Zelmer, Adopting Inflation Targeting: Practical Issues for Emerging Market Countries (2000)
SOURCE · IMF Occasional Paper · publication page and full text →

Drawing on the experiences of Brazil, Chile, the Czech Republic, Israel, Poland and South Africa, the study examines the target, legal mandate, decision process, forecasting capacity, accountability arrangements and communications required to implement inflation targeting. It provides the principal operational reference in this section.

Recommended focus: Executive summary and the sections on institutional arrangements, target design and communications.

6
Nicoletta Batini, Kenneth Kuttner and Douglas Laxton, "Does Inflation Targeting Work in Emerging Markets?" (World Economic Outlook, Chapter 4, September 2005)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · World Economic Outlook chapter →

Using a large cross-country sample, the chapter finds that inflation targeting in emerging markets has been associated with lower inflation and inflation volatility without a discernible cost to output volatility, once adopted under adequate institutional preconditions. It gives the Board an accessible empirical answer to whether the framework Armenia adopted has actually worked elsewhere.

Recommended focus: The findings on emerging market performance and the discussion of preconditions for successful adoption; the technical appendix may be omitted.

7
Nicoletta Batini and Douglas Laxton, "Under What Conditions Can Inflation Targeting Be Adopted? The Experience of Emerging Markets" (2007), in Frederic S. Mishkin and Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel, eds., Monetary Policy Under Inflation Targeting (Santiago: Central Bank of Chile)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Chile · working paper version →

Batini and Laxton set out the institutional, fiscal and financial preconditions an emerging market economy should meet before adopting inflation targeting, and examine what happens when countries adopt the framework before those preconditions are fully in place. The paper complements Schaechter, Stone and Zelmer's operational account with a more analytical treatment of readiness.

Recommended focus: The statement of preconditions and the comparative evidence on early versus late adopters; the econometric sections may be omitted.

8
Laurence Ball, "The Case for a Long-Run Inflation Target of Four Percent" (IMF Working Paper 14/92, 2014)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · working paper in full →

Ball argues that a higher long-run inflation target than the conventional 2 percent gives a central bank more room to cut interest rates before hitting the effective lower bound, at a modest cost in terms of the distortions higher inflation itself creates. The paper gives the Board direct exposure to the live debate over the appropriate target level, relevant given the CBA's own target has been revised over time.

Recommended focus: The statement of the trade-off and the concluding assessment of the appropriate target range; the formal model may be omitted.

9
CENTRAL BANK REFERENCE
Bank of Canada, "Renewal of the Inflation-Control Target: Background Information" (November 2011)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official background document →

The document records the Bank of Canada's own periodic review of its inflation-control target, including the analytical work and criteria considered before renewing the existing target rather than changing it. It provides a concrete institutional precedent for how a central bank conducts and documents a target review, relevant to the CBA's own annual review of its Statement of Long-Run Monetary Policy Objectives.

Recommended focus: The summary of the review process and the criteria considered; the background research annexes may be treated as supporting material.

10
Thomas J. Sargent, "The Ends of Four Big Inflations" (1982)
SOURCE · NBER book chapter and full text →

Sargent's comparative historical cases illustrate why a durable nominal stabilisation may require a credible change in the broader monetary and fiscal regime. Although the episodes are more extreme than the environment faced by a modern inflation targeting central bank, the institutional lesson is directly relevant: monetary policy cannot indefinitely offset an inconsistent fiscal framework.

Recommended focus: The opening argument, the comparative case narratives and the final synthesis; technical details may be omitted.

11
Alberto Alesina and Lawrence H. Summers, "Central Bank Independence and Macroeconomic Performance: Some Comparative Evidence" (1993)
SOURCE · JSTOR stable article page →

The comparative evidence provides a foundational reference on the relationship between central bank independence and inflation performance. It supports consideration of the distinction between legal independence, operational independence, accountability and the practical credibility of the institution.

Recommended focus: The full article; it is brief and suitable for a single Board preparation session.

12
Alan S. Blinder, Michael Ehrmann, Marcel Fratzscher, Jakob de Haan and David-Jan Jansen, "Central Bank Communication and Monetary Policy: A Survey of Theory and Evidence" (2008)
SOURCE · NBER working paper and full text →

The survey establishes communication as part of the transmission mechanism rather than an auxiliary public relations function. It distinguishes the audiences and objectives of central bank communication and examines the choices among transparency, clarity, predictability and effective deliberation.

Recommended focus: Introduction, the sections on policy effectiveness and accountability, and the concluding principles.

13
Ben S. Bernanke, Forecasting for Monetary Policy Making and Communication at the Bank of England: A Review (2024)
SOURCE · Bank of England · official review in full →

Bernanke's review is a contemporary institutional case study of how forecasts should support policy decisions and communication under heightened uncertainty. Its discussion of alternative scenarios, forecast infrastructure, supply side analysis and the limits of a single central projection has direct relevance for the CBA's evolution toward risk based decision making.

Recommended focus: Executive summary and the recommendations concerning scenarios, decision support and communication.

14
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Piti Disyatat, "Targeting Inflation (More) Flexibly" (2024)
SOURCE · BIS central bank speech and full text →

Disyatat assesses flexible inflation targeting after three decades of international experience. The speech distinguishes commitment to the nominal anchor from mechanical attainment of the target over a short horizon and explains how judgement, financial conditions and real economy considerations may be incorporated without weakening credibility.

Recommended focus: The full speech; it is short and written for a policy audience.

15
P1 · FIRSTHAND TESTIMONY
Paul A. Volcker, Statement before the Joint Economic Committee (17 October 1979)
SOURCE · FRASER, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis · official statement in full →

Delivered eleven days after the Federal Reserve announced its October 1979 changes to operating procedures, the testimony records the case for breaking inflationary expectations, demonstrating that monetary policy would not validate continuing inflation and sustaining restraint despite substantial costs in the short term. The reasoning was presented before the outcome of the policy change was known.

Recommended focus: The opening diagnosis, the explanation of the 6 October measures and the concluding discussion of policy persistence and fiscal support.

II. Monetary policy transmission and external constraints in a small
16
Ben S. Bernanke and Mark Gertler, "Inside the Black Box: The Credit Channel of Monetary Policy Transmission" (1995)
SOURCE · American Economic Association · full article →

Bernanke and Gertler provide the foundational conceptual account of how monetary policy affects borrowing conditions through bank balance sheets, borrower net worth and the external finance premium. The framework supports analysis of transmission in a financial system centred on banks, particularly when risk perceptions or collateral values change rapidly.

Recommended focus: The conceptual description of the balance sheet and bank lending channels; formal details may be omitted.

17
Jacob A. Frenkel, "Monetary Policy: Domestic Targets and International Constraints" (1983)
SOURCE · NBER working paper and full text →

Frenkel's brief and foundational paper explains how openness changes the information set, constraints and instruments available to a central bank. It addresses foreign exchange intervention, sterilisation and the role of exchange rate information in monetary decisions without requiring a large formal framework.

Recommended focus: The full paper, with particular attention to intervention and the role of exchange rates in policy design.

18
Maurice Obstfeld, "Trilemmas and Trade-offs: Living with Financial Globalisation" (2015)
SOURCE · BIS Working Paper · full text →

Obstfeld reassesses the scope for monetary autonomy when capital is mobile and global financial conditions transmit strongly across borders. The central lesson is balanced: a flexible exchange rate preserves meaningful policy space, but does not provide complete insulation from external financial shocks. Complementary macroprudential and financial policies therefore remain important.

Recommended focus: Introduction, the discussion of the monetary trilemma and the concluding policy policy choices.

19
Hélène Rey, "Dilemma not Trilemma: The Global Financial Cycle and Monetary Policy Independence" (2013)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City · Jackson Hole paper in full →

Rey's Jackson Hole paper places the global financial cycle at the centre of the policy problem. It shows why capital flows, leverage and risky asset prices may respond to global conditions even under floating exchange rates. The paper provides the conceptual basis for considering macroprudential measures and capital flow tools alongside the policy rate.

Recommended focus: The opening diagnosis, the policy implications and the conclusion; econometric sections may be treated as supporting material.

20
Bank for International Settlements, "Monetary Policy Frameworks in EMEs: Inflation Targeting, the Exchange Rate and Financial Stability" (2019)
SOURCE · BIS Annual Economic Report chapter · full text →

The chapter provides a comprehensive practical synthesis for central banks in emerging markets. It explains why many inflation targeting institutions combine exchange rate flexibility with foreign exchange intervention and macroprudential tools, and how currency depreciation affects inflation, balance sheets and domestic financial conditions.

Recommended focus: Key takeaways and the sections on exchange rate transmission, the financial channel and the policy tool mix.

21
Giancarlo Corsetti, Keith Kuester and Gernot J. Müller, "In a Great Recession, the Case for Flexible Exchange Rates Is Alive and Well" (2017)
SOURCE · CEPR policy summary · full text →

Corsetti, Kuester and Müller apply the classical case for exchange rate flexibility to a severe global downturn. The analysis informs the Armenian experience from 2008 to 2012 by treating the exchange rate as a shock absorber whose effectiveness depends on the nature of the external shock and the constraints on domestic and foreign monetary policy.

Recommended focus: The full policy summary; the underlying technical paper is not required.

22
Michael McLeay, Amar Radia and Ryland Thomas, "Money Creation in the Modern Economy" (2014)
SOURCE · Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin · full text →

The article provides an institutional account of deposit creation by commercial banks and the implementation of interest rate policy by the central bank. It supports a proper interpretation of reserves, money growth, the bank lending channel, liquidity operations and monetary transmission.

Recommended focus: The full article, especially the distinction between money creation and the constraints on bank lending.

23
Central Bank of Armenia, Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: Theory and Practice at the Central Bank of Armenia (2026)
SOURCE · CBA publication · full book →

The volume is the principal CBA reference for the current framework. It presents the rationale for multiple scenarios, deliberation based on risk, enhanced analytical tools and the associated transparency and accountability arrangements. It connects the general literature with the responsibilities of the Board under the CBA framework.

Recommended focus: Executive overview and the chapters on scenario design, decision making, communication and accountability.

24
P2 · FIRSTHAND INTERVIEW
Jacob A. Frenkel, "Interview with Jacob Frenkel" (1993)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis · full interview →

Speaking while Governor of the Bank of Israel, Frenkel explains Israel's stabilisation experience, the joint role of fiscal responsibility and a nominal anchor, the transition to a crawling exchange rate band and the limits of foreign exchange intervention when underlying policies are inconsistent. The interview combines technical authority with direct institutional experience.

Recommended focus: The sections on Israel's inflation stabilisation, the crawling band, central bank independence and the choice of exchange rate regime.

25
P3 · FIRSTHAND SPEECH
Stanley Fischer, "Monetary Policy in the United States and in Developing Countries" (30 June 2015)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Drawing on experience as Governor of the Bank of Israel, IMF First Deputy Managing Director and Federal Reserve Vice Chair, Fischer addresses the design of monetary frameworks in developing economies. He gives particular attention to external shocks, capital mobility, exchange rate management, shallow financial markets and the institutional preconditions for effective interest rate transmission.

Recommended focus: "U.S. Monetary Policy Spillovers and Global Interest Rates" and "Monetary Policy in Developing Countries."

26
P4 · FIRSTHAND LECTURE
Agustín Carstens, "Exchange Rates and Monetary Policy Frameworks in Emerging Market Economies" (2 May 2019)
SOURCE · Bank for International Settlements · official lecture and slides →

Carstens brings the perspective of a former Governor of the Bank of Mexico and BIS General Manager to the interaction among inflation targeting, exchange rate movements, financial stability and foreign exchange intervention. The lecture explains why central banks in emerging markets may use a broader policy toolkit without abandoning the domestic nominal anchor.

Recommended focus: The sections on exchange rate channels, policy frameworks and the role of foreign exchange intervention.

III. Armenia's experience under inflation targeting
27
CBA PRIMARY SOURCE
Douglas Laxton, Hayk Avetisyan and Vahe Avagyan, eds., "Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: Theory and Practice at the Central Bank of Armenia" (2026)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · full book →

Chapter 1 of the CBA volume provides the Bank's own narrative history of monetary policy in Armenia, from the introduction of the dram amid hyperinflation in 1993, through monetary aggregate targeting from 1994 to 2005, the adoption of full inflation targeting in January 2006, and the subsequent evolution of the target. It supplies the connected institutional narrative that the primary case-study reports below document only episode by episode.

Recommended focus: Chapter 1, History of Monetary Policy at the CBA, in full; the later chapters on the current risk management framework are covered elsewhere in this reading list.

28
Hayk Avetisyan, Haykaz Igityan and Anzhela Papikyan, "Inflation Target in Armenia" (Central Bank of Armenia, 2024)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · official analytical material →

The CBA staff analysis traces the record of Armenia's 4 percent inflation target since its adoption in 2006, the inflation outcomes actually achieved, and the reduction of the target in 2025. It complements Chapter 1 of the CBA volume above with a focused account of target design and performance specifically, rather than the institutional history more broadly.

Recommended focus: The full analysis; it is concise and written for a general institutional audience.

29
Guillermo A. Calvo, "Capital Flows and Capital-Market Crises: The Simple Economics of Sudden Stops" (1998)
SOURCE · Journal of Applied Economics · full article →

Calvo provides the foundational conceptual account of sudden stops in capital inflows. The reading is directly relevant to Armenia's experience during the global financial crisis, when changes in external financing, remittances, risk premia and exchange rate expectations interacted with domestic balance sheets and financial stability.

Recommended focus: The conceptual mechanism and the discussion of policy vulnerabilities; technical derivations may be omitted.

30
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Laurence H. Meyer, "Monetary Policy Objectives and Strategy" (1996)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Meyer's speech provides the original policymaker account of "opportunistic disinflation": maintaining vigilance against renewed inflation while allowing favourable supply conditions or weaker demand to secure a lower inflation rate at reduced output cost. For the 2014 to 2015 Armenian case, it helps distinguish temporary imported price relief from a durable reduction in underlying inflation and expectations.

Recommended focus: The discussion of opportunistic disinflation and the concluding statement of monetary policy priorities.

31
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Alan Greenspan, "Risk and Uncertainty in Monetary Policy" (2004)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Greenspan's address examines decision making when models are incomplete, probabilities are uncertain and some outcomes are disproportionately costly. It provides a framework for Board consideration of preemptive action, optionality and the treatment of risks that have low probability but potentially severe consequences.

Recommended focus: The discussion of risk management, model uncertainty and policy responses to asymmetric costs.

32
PRIMARY CBA CASE STUDY
Case 1: Global Financial Crisis and European debt crisis, 2008 to 2012
SOURCE · CBA Monetary Policy Program and Inflation Report, Q4 2008 →  ·  SOURCE · CBA Board decision of 3 March 2009 →

Read the report together with the March 2009 decision to examine the shift in external financing, the role of exchange rate flexibility, the return to a floating regime and the coordination of price stability and financial stability considerations.

33
P5 · FIRSTHAND LECTURE AND VIDEO
Ben S. Bernanke, "The Federal Reserve's Response to the Financial Crisis" (27 March 2012)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official video, transcript and slides →

Bernanke reconstructs the diagnosis and actions of the Federal Reserve during the global financial crisis from the perspective of the Chair who led the response. Consideration together with the CBA's contemporaneous records from 2008 and 2009 permits comparison between the constraints facing a reserve currency central bank and those facing a small open economy.

34
PRIMARY CBA CASE STUDY
Case 2: Russian crisis and regional spillovers, 2014 to 2015
SOURCE · CBA Inflation Report, Q1 2015 →

The report documents the depreciation of the Russian ruble, the reduction in remittances and foreign currency inflows, pressures in Armenia's foreign exchange market, the response of inflation expectations and the sequence of CBA policy actions.

35
P6 · FIRSTHAND SPEECH
Elvira Nabiullina, Address to the State Duma on the Bank of Russia's 2015 Performance (14 June 2016)
SOURCE · Bank of Russia · official address in full →

As the Governor who led the Bank of Russia through the 2014 to 2015 oil price, sanctions and exchange rate shock, Nabiullina provides a retrospective account of the move to a floating ruble, the increase in the key rate to 17 percent and the subsequent disinflation. This is a direct regional comparator for examining exchange rate adjustment, inflation expectations and financial stability risks.

36
PRIMARY CBA CASE STUDY
Case 3: COVID 19 pandemic and the 2020 Nagorno Karabakh war
SOURCE · CBA Inflation Report, Q4 2020 →

The report records the simultaneous demand, supply, exchange rate, risk premium and uncertainty shocks confronting the CBA. It documents the basis on which the policy stance remained supportive while the Board raised the refinancing rate to contain prospective inflation and inflation expectations.

37
P7 · CONTEMPORANEOUS CBA BOARD RECORD
Central Bank of Armenia, refinancing rate decision of 15 December 2020
SOURCE · CBA · official decision and policy rationale →

The decision records why the Board raised the refinancing rate by one percentage point despite weak activity and below target inflation. It should be used as the durable official companion to Governor Martin Galstyan's policy rate press conference cited in the CBA's prudent risk management volume.

38
PRIMARY CBA CASE STUDY
Case 4: Russia and Ukraine conflict and subsequent inflows, 2022 to 2023
SOURCE · CBA Inflation Report, Q1 2022 →  ·  SOURCE · IMF 2023 Article IV Consultation · full staff report →

Considered together, the CBA report and the subsequent IMF review provide a prospective and retrospective account of the episode. The CBA report presents the initial multiple scenario assessment under exceptional uncertainty. The IMF review documents the realised inflows, appreciation, demand strength, inflation dynamics and the effects of the CBA's preemptive tightening and subsequent gradual normalisation.

39
P8 · FIRSTHAND PRESS CONFERENCE
Jerome H. Powell, FOMC Press Conference (15 June 2022)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official transcript in full →

The press conference records the Federal Reserve's decision to accelerate tightening as inflation broadened and measures of inflation expectations became more concerning. It documents the global policy shock facing Armenia in 2022, the balance between guidance and flexibility, and the judgment required when the risks of doing too much and too little were both material.

IV. Bridge to the current framework and special viewing
40
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Martin Galstyan, "Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: The Role of Policy Credibility" (IMF Annual Meetings, 13 October 2022)
SOURCE · IMF Governor Talk · event page, recording and summary →

Governor Galstyan sets out the motivation for treating monetary policy as a risk management exercise organised around multiple plausible scenarios rather than a single most likely baseline. The discussion also addresses credibility, nonlinearity, forecast error, human capital requirements and the communication challenges associated with the transition.

Recommended focus: The full 30 minute session.

41
P9 · FIRSTHAND LECTURE · CBA REFERENCE
Stephen S. Poloz, "Monetary Policy in Unknowable Times" (25 May 2020)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official lecture and PDF →

Poloz distinguishes measurable risk from uncertainty that cannot be reduced to reliable probabilities and explains the implications for policy models, judgment, contingency planning and communication. Delivered by a serving governor during the COVID 19 shock, the account provides a direct connection to the CBA's multiple scenario framework.

Recommended focus: The discussion of risk, uncertainty and the practical conduct of policy when the distribution of outcomes is not knowable.

42
P10 · FIRSTHAND SPEECH · CBA REFERENCE
Christian Hawkesby, "A Least Regrets Approach to Uncertainty: Hawks, Doves and the White Heron" (21 September 2021)
SOURCE · Reserve Bank of New Zealand · official speech and PDF →

Hawkesby explains how the Reserve Bank of New Zealand used scenarios and a least regrets criterion during the pandemic, including why severe downside risks initially justified rapid action and why the balance of risks later shifted. The speech provides an operational precedent for the approach discussed in the CBA volume.

Recommended focus: "Risk Management and a Least Regrets Approach" and the account of its application during COVID 19.

43
P11 · FIRSTHAND ARTICLE · CBA REFERENCE
James Bullard, "A Risk Management Approach to Monetary Policy" (2021)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis · full article →

Writing while President of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and an FOMC participant, Bullard applies a perspective based on scenarios and risk management to the unexpectedly strong U.S. recovery and inflation of 2021. The CBA foreword identifies him among the policy thinkers advocating changes to monetary policy practice in response to uncertainty.

Recommended focus: The comparison of baseline and upside scenarios and the implications for earlier policy normalisation.

44
P12 · FIRSTHAND SPEECH · CBA REFERENCE
Jerome H. Powell, "Monetary Policy and Risk Management at a Time of Low Inflation and Low Unemployment" (2 October 2018)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Powell presents risk management as the practical task of balancing the danger of moving too quickly against the danger of moving too slowly when key economic concepts are uncertain. Read alongside his June 2022 press conference, the speech shows how the same decision discipline must adapt when the inflation environment changes materially.

Recommended focus: The discussion of uncertain estimates, policy errors on both sides and the role of gradualism.

45
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Mark Carney, "Principled and Pragmatic: Canada's Path" (World Economic Forum Annual Meeting, 20 January 2026)
SOURCE · World Economic Forum · official address and transcript →

Carney's address examines the strategic environment confronting small and middle powers. It addresses fragmentation, the coercive use of economic integration, vulnerabilities in supply chains and finance, the cost of resilience and the need to combine principles with pragmatic risk management.

Recommended focus: The sections on strategic autonomy, resilience, diversification and collective action by middle powers.

V. Deeper reference
46
Ben S. Bernanke, Thomas Laubach, Frederic S. Mishkin and Adam S. Posen, Inflation Targeting: Lessons from the International Experience (Princeton University Press, 1999)
SOURCE · Princeton University Press · publisher page →

Bernanke, Laubach, Mishkin and Posen provide the principal early academic study of inflation targeting, examining the experience of nine countries in depth. It remains the standard scholarly reference for the framework and the intellectual point of departure for most of the country-specific literature elsewhere in this reading list. Unlike the other sources here, the volume is a print academic book without a freely accessible full text online, and is provided as the main reference for detailed study rather than an assigned Board reading.

Recommended focus: Not applicable; provided as a reference volume rather than assigned reading.

Source links were verified on 10 August 2026. Availability may subsequently change on publisher or institutional websites.

I. The CBA framework and its operational record
1
CORE CBA REFERENCE
Douglas Laxton, Hayk Avetisyan and Vahe Avagyan, eds., Prudent Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: Theory and Practice at the Central Bank of Armenia (2026)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · official book in full →

The CBA volume is the governing reference for Part III. It sets out the intellectual case for policymaking guided by the principle of least regrets, the taxonomy and use of scenarios, FPAS Mark II, analytical tools, institutional processes, human capital arrangements, communications and the accountability framework.

Recommended focus: Introduction; Chapters 3 and 5 to 7; and Appendices A to C. Other chapters may be assigned according to the Board member's responsibilities.

2
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Martin Galstyan, "Risk Management Approach to Price Stability: The Role of Policy Credibility" (IMF Annual Meetings, 13 October 2022)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · official Governor Talk, summary and recording →

Governor Galstyan presents the original policy case for moving from a single most probable baseline toward multiple plausible scenarios and least regrets decision making. The discussion directly addresses credibility, nonlinearity, forecast error, human capital and communication.

Recommended focus: The full 30 minute session and the accompanying presentation.

3
IMF WORKING PAPER · CBA FRAMEWORK PRECURSOR
Ali Alichi, Kevin Clinton, Charles Freedman, Ondra Kamenik, Michel Juillard, Douglas Laxton, Jarkko Turunen and Hou Wang, "Avoiding Dark Corners: A Robust Monetary Policy Framework for the United States" (IMF Working Paper 15/134, 2015)
SOURCE · International Monetary Fund · full working paper →

The paper sets out the original "dark corners" framework, combining an optimal control approach with risk management and improved communication for United States monetary policy following the global financial crisis. It is the direct precursor to the CBA's own formulation of the same concept, applied seven years later to Armenia.

Recommended focus: The abstract, introduction and the discussion of the risk management approach to policy; the technical model sections may be omitted.

4
David Archer, Martin Galstyan and Douglas Laxton, "FPAS Mark II: Avoiding Dark Corners and Eliminating the Folly in Baselines and Local Approximations" (2022)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · publication page and full paper →

The paper records an early formulation of monetary policy as risk management at the CBA. It explains the rejection of an "expert forecaster" posture, the meaning of dark corners and the institutional purpose of analysis based on scenarios.

Recommended focus: Abstract, introduction, the conceptual discussion of dark corners and the institutional conclusions; model details may be omitted.

5
PRIMARY CBA POLICY RECORD
Central Bank of Armenia, Monetary Policy Report and Transparency Report package
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · current monetary policy reports and decision packages →

The current policy package documents PRMAPS in operation. It presents the construction of the market reference scenario, the Case A and Case B risks, the relationship between those risks and the policy stance, attributed Board deliberations, votes and vote explanations.

Recommended focus: The latest quarterly Monetary Policy Report, Executive Monetary Policy Statement and Transparency Report issued on the same day.

6
PRIMARY CBA INSTITUTIONAL SOURCE
Hayk Avetisyan, Haykaz Igityan and Anzhela Papikyan, "Inflation Target in Armenia" (Central Bank of Armenia, 2024)
SOURCE · Central Bank of Armenia · official analytical material →

The CBA staff analysis records Armenia's 4 percent inflation target since 2006, the average outcomes achieved over that period and the subsequent reduction of the target, situating the current PRMAPS framework within the CBA's longer inflation-targeting record.

Recommended focus: The full analysis; it is concise and written for a general institutional audience.

II. Monetary policy under uncertainty and the least regrets principle
7
William C. Brainard, "Uncertainty and the Effectiveness of Policy" (1967)
SOURCE · American Economic Review, Papers and Proceedings · full article →

Brainard's foundational result, now known as the Brainard conservatism principle, shows that uncertainty about the structure of the economy should generally lead a policymaker to act more cautiously rather than to disregard the uncertainty. The paper is the academic origin of the caution that the policymaker accounts later in this Part describe in practice.

Recommended focus: The statement of the central result and its policy interpretation; the formal derivation may be read selectively.

8
Robert J. Barro and David B. Gordon, "Rules, Discretion and Reputation in a Model of Monetary Policy" (1983)
SOURCE · National Bureau of Economic Research · working paper in full →

Barro and Gordon show that a central bank with full discretion will tend toward a persistently higher inflation rate than announced, and argue that binding rules or reputational commitment are needed to overcome this bias. The paper is the classical case for rules over discretionary judgment, included so that Board members encounter the strongest counterargument to a scenario-based, discretionary framework before considering why the CBA has chosen its present approach.

Recommended focus: The statement of the discretion problem and the case for rules in the introduction and conclusion; the equilibrium derivations may be omitted.

9
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Alan Greenspan, "Risk and Uncertainty in Monetary Policy" (3 January 2004)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Greenspan provides the foundational policymaker statement that uncertainty is the defining characteristic of the monetary policy landscape. He explains why policy must consider distributions of outcomes, asymmetric costs, robustness and the limitations of both models and simple rules.

Recommended focus: The sections beginning with uncertainty as the defining characteristic of policy and the discussion of risk management, robustness and judgment.

10
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Stephen S. Poloz, "Monetary Policy as Risk Management" (12 December 2013)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official speech and PDF →

Delivered early in Poloz's governorship, the speech explains how a flexible inflation targeting central bank balances risks to inflation, economic activity and financial stability. It presents risk management as an organized discipline for policy formulation.

Recommended focus: The sections on policy formulation, the two risk lenses and the practical policy example.

11
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Stephen S. Poloz, "Integrating Uncertainty and Monetary Policy-Making: A Practitioner's Perspective" (2014)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official discussion paper and full PDF →

Poloz develops the operational argument that fundamental uncertainty must be incorporated explicitly into policy formulation rather than appended mechanically to a baseline forecast. The paper connects coherent modelling, judgment, risk narratives and two way market pricing.

Recommended focus: Introduction, the practitioner discussion of fundamental uncertainty and the concluding implications for policy formulation and communication.

12
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Stephen S. Poloz, "Monetary Policy in Unknowable Times" (25 May 2020)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official lecture and PDF →

Poloz distinguishes measurable risk from uncertainty that cannot be represented by reliable probabilities. Delivered during the COVID 19 shock, the lecture explains the implications for contingency planning, policy judgment, models and communication when the future is genuinely unknowable.

Recommended focus: The full lecture, particularly the distinction among knowns, unknowns and unknowable outcomes.

13
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Jerome H. Powell, "Monetary Policy and Risk Management at a Time of Low Inflation and Low Unemployment" (2 October 2018)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Powell frames policy as a balance between the risk of moving too rapidly and the risk of moving too slowly when estimates of slack and equilibrium are uncertain. The speech examines gradualism, robustness and the consequences of policy errors in either direction.

Recommended focus: The discussion of uncertain economic estimates, policy errors on both sides and the risk management basis for gradual adjustment.

14
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Christian Hawkesby, "A Least Regrets Approach to Uncertainty: Hawks, Doves and the White Heron" (21 September 2021)
SOURCE · Reserve Bank of New Zealand · official speech and PDF →

Hawkesby explains the application of a least regrets criterion at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. He documents the use of severe downside scenarios during the pandemic and the subsequent shift in the balance of risks as the recovery strengthened.

Recommended focus: "Risk Management and a Least Regrets Approach" and the account of its application during COVID 19.

15
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
James Bullard, "A Risk Management Approach to Monetary Policy" (2021)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis · full article →

Writing as an FOMC participant, Bullard applies scenario based risk management to the unexpectedly strong recovery and inflation of 2021. The article illustrates how a material upside scenario can justify retaining policy optionality and preparing for earlier normalization.

Recommended focus: The comparison of baseline and upside scenarios and the resulting policy implications.

16
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Christine Lagarde, "Policymaking in an Age of Shifts and Breaks" (25 August 2023)
SOURCE · European Central Bank · official Jackson Hole speech in full →

Lagarde explains why structural changes in geopolitics, energy, trade and labour markets may break previously stable economic relationships. Her proposed principles of clarity, flexibility and humility provide a senior policymaker's formulation of robust decision making under structural uncertainty.

Recommended focus: The opening diagnosis and the concluding section on clarity, flexibility and humility.

17
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Ben S. Bernanke, Forecasting for Monetary Policy Making and Communication at the Bank of England: A Review (2024)
SOURCE · Bank of England · official independent review in full →

Bernanke's independent review is a leading institutional assessment of how forecasts should support decisions and communications after major forecast failures. It recommends stronger infrastructure, clearer distinctions between central projections and alternative scenarios, and a more effective account of policy risks.

Recommended focus: Executive summary and the recommendations on scenarios, decision support, forecast infrastructure and communication.

18
Douglas Laxton, Haykaz Igityan and Shalva Mkhatrishvili, "Monetary Policy Credibility, Avoiding Dark Corners, and Risk Management: A Response to Ben Bernanke's Review" (2025)
SOURCE · Oxford Review of Economic Policy · article page →

The article connects Bernanke's review with the systems based on scenarios that were developed in Armenia and Georgia. Its principal contribution is the argument that scenario analysis must be combined with an explicit strategy for protecting endogenous policy credibility.

Recommended focus: Introduction, the institutional comparison and the policy conclusions; technical model sections are optional.

19
Lawrence H. Summers, "The Scientific Illusion in Empirical Macroeconomics" (1991)
SOURCE · Author's official publication page →

Summers cautions against equating technical sophistication with reliable policy knowledge. The essay is included as a conceptual challenge to false precision and as a reminder that historical comparison, institutional knowledge and disciplined judgment remain essential in macroeconomic policy.

Recommended focus: The full essay; it is conceptual and may be read without technical appendices.

III. Scenarios, robust analysis and institutional judgment
20
Pierre Wack, "Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead" (1985)
SOURCE · Harvard Business Review · article page →

Wack's account of scenario planning at Royal Dutch/Shell defines scenarios as instruments for changing the decision maker's perception of plausible futures rather than as competing forecasts. The case demonstrates the importance of scenario analysis when inherited regularities no longer provide dependable guidance.

Recommended focus: The discussion of forecast failure, decision maker engagement and the Shell oil shock case.

21
Paul J. H. Schoemaker, "Scenario Planning: A Tool for Strategic Thinking" (1995)
SOURCE · MIT Sloan Management Review · article page →

Schoemaker provides a disciplined account of how to identify basic trends, critical uncertainties and internally coherent scenarios. The approach distinguishes a manageable set of scenarios relevant to the decision from an undisciplined catalogue of possibilities.

Recommended focus: The scenario construction process and the discussion of overconfidence and tunnel vision.

22
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Andrew G. Haldane and Vasileios Madouros, "The Dog and the Frisbee" (2012)
SOURCE · Bank of England · official paper and full PDF →

Haldane and Madouros use the period following the crisis regulatory experience to show why greater complexity does not necessarily produce better decisions in complex systems. The broader lesson for monetary policy is to retain analytical discipline while avoiding the presumption that a more elaborate model automatically provides a more robust answer.

Recommended focus: The conceptual argument and policy conclusions; detailed regulatory illustrations may be read selectively.

23
CBA REFERENCE
Edward de Bono, Lateral Thinking: A Textbook of Creativity (1970)
SOURCE · Open Library · bibliographic record and controlled preview →

The CBA volume invokes de Bono's lateral and parallel thinking as a practical discipline for generating alternatives before converging on a policy judgment. The relevance is institutional rather than psychological: Board and staff discussions should be structured to surface distinct interpretations instead of rewarding early consensus.

Recommended focus: The introductory explanation of lateral thinking and the exercises on generating alternative approaches.

IV. Governance, Board process and institutional capability
24
Central Bank Governance Group, Issues in the Governance of Central Banks (2009)
SOURCE · Bank for International Settlements · report page and full PDF →

The report is the principal international reference on central bank governance. It covers mandates, legal status, decision structures, relations with government, accountability, risk management and organizational arrangements, while recognizing that institutional design must reflect national circumstances.

Recommended focus: Highlights and Chapters 4, 7 and 9 on decision structures, accountability and organizational arrangements.

25
Charles A. E. Goodhart, "The Changing Role of Central Banks" (2010)
SOURCE · Bank for International Settlements · working paper and full PDF →

Goodhart places changing central bank mandates and institutional design within a broad historical perspective. The paper examines the interaction among price stability, financial stability, balance sheet responsibilities and relations with government when the operating environment changes.

Recommended focus: The historical overview and the concluding discussion of mandates, instruments and relations with government.

26
Alan S. Blinder, "Monetary Policy by Committee: Why and How?" (2005)
SOURCE · Princeton University, Center for Economic Policy Studies · working paper in full →

Blinder examines why most central banks now set policy through a committee rather than a single governor, and what distinguishes an effective policy committee from an ineffective one. The paper addresses collective decision making directly, a question distinct from the independence and mandate design covered elsewhere in this Part.

Recommended focus: The account of why committees are used and the discussion of what makes a committee function well; the experimental evidence section is optional.

27
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE
Ben S. Bernanke, "Central Bank Independence, Transparency, and Accountability" (25 May 2010)
SOURCE · Federal Reserve Board · official speech in full →

Bernanke explains why operational independence must be accompanied by transparency, democratic accountability and a clear division between politically established objectives and the conduct of policy. These principles bear directly on the responsibilities of individual Board members within a collective public institution.

Recommended focus: The sections on the case for independence and the obligations of transparency and accountability.

V. Communication, transparency and accountability
28
Alan S. Blinder, Michael Ehrmann, Marcel Fratzscher, Jakob de Haan and David-Jan Jansen, "Central Bank Communication and Monetary Policy: A Survey of Theory and Evidence" (2008)
SOURCE · National Bureau of Economic Research · working paper and full text →

The synthesis explains how communication influences expectations, market pricing, policy effectiveness and accountability. It also examines the choices among clarity, transparency, predictability, individual expression and effective internal deliberation.

Recommended focus: Introduction, sections on policy effectiveness and accountability, and the concluding principles.

29
POLICY AUTHOR
Frederic S. Mishkin, "Can Central Bank Transparency Go Too Far?" (2004)
SOURCE · Reserve Bank of Australia · conference paper in full →

Mishkin provides a disciplined counterweight to the assumption that more disclosure is always better. He argues that transparency should be evaluated by whether it improves understanding, accountability and the pursuit of long term objectives rather than by the volume of information released.

Recommended focus: The framing of the transparency question and the concluding discussion of simplicity, honesty about policy choices and long term objectives.

30
FIRSTHAND POLICYMAKER SOURCE · CBA REFERENCE
Stephen S. Poloz, "Let Me Be Clear: From Transparency to Trust and Understanding" (27 June 2018)
SOURCE · Bank of Canada · official speech and PDF →

Poloz distinguishes the release of information from genuine public understanding. He addresses audience segmentation, plain language, open models and data, visual communication, social media and the importance of listening to the public as well as explaining policy to it.

International Monetary Fund, The Central Bank Transparency Code (2020)

The IMF Code provides the principal international benchmark for transparency across governance, policies, operations, outcomes and official relations. PRIMARY CBA INSTITUTIONAL SOURCE
Central Bank of Armenia, Monetary Policy Communications Framework (2024)
